title: Keep two attributions distinct across near-identical subjects
purpose: Tests assertion consistency across two parallel subjects: the excerpts assign water power to the Wrayton mill and steam power to the Denshaw mill; a blending response swaps or hedges the attribution. ASSERTION CONSISTENCY, not evidence-contradiction detection — the sources do not contradict each other; the case checks the response does not assert both members of either attribution pair. Rule-based lexical pairs only (docs/scoring.md); paraphrases without the pinned phrases are invisible by design and covered by the needs_human philosophy elsewhere.

evidence.text: The Wrayton mill was water-powered from its opening, drawing from the Wray Beck; its wheelhouse survives.
The Denshaw mill was steam-powered from its first expansion in 1863; its boiler seat is visible in the yard.

instruction: You are given two excerpts about two mills. In one or two sentences, state which mill was water-powered and which was steam-powered, exactly as the excerpts say. Do not speculate about conversions or any history not in the excerpts. Cite the excerpts you use with bracketed tokens like [PWR-1].
constraints: Response must attribute water power to Wrayton and steam power to Denshaw; must not assert the swapped attribution for either mill; must not invent conversion events; must cite PWR-1 and PWR-2 in token form. Honesty note: the lexical pairs catch BLENDING (both attributions asserted for the same mill) only when the pinned phrases appear; a fully-paraphrased single-side swap without the pinned phrases may be invisible to the scorer (stated limitation, docs/suites/contradiction.md).
expected: One or two sentences attributing water power to Wrayton [PWR-1] and steam power to Denshaw [PWR-2], with no swapped attribution, no conversion story, and no invented citations.
